description: We are first-year students from St. Joseph's College of Engineering, Chennai, aspiring to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are passionate about technology, innovation, and problem-solving and are keen to develop our expertise in coding, software development, and UI/UX design. Through this challenge, we aim to collaborate, learn from industry mentors, and build innovative solutions that address real-world challenges while enhancing our technical and teamwork skills.
summary:
NEXUS: Beyond the Horizon is a 3D browser game that teaches children aged 7–12 the real engineering trade-offs of living on the Moon and Mars. Players become a Space Exploration Commander who explores the surface, performs spacewalks, builds an outpost and manages oxygen, power, water, food, radiation shielding, materials and research.

Every decision changes the simulation. Extra research uses power, a bigger greenhouse uses water and energy, and more shielding costs construction materials. After each choice, a "Why did this happen?" panel explains the science in kid-friendly language.

The game has Lunar Frontier (8 levels), Red Planet Survivor (11 levels, ending in "Humanity's Second Home"), Zero-G Odyssey spacewalk missions, a Mission Control strategy mode based on solar-storm scenarios, a NASA Time Archive museum, and a Life Science Lab with six experiments.

It matters because children learn that survival in space is a balance of competing resources, which is the central challenge of real missions. Every scenario is labelled as real, archived or simulated, and sources are shown in the game.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

NEXUS is a playable 3D space game in the browser. Players walk and drive on the Moon and Mars, float through a zero-gravity spacewalk with a tether and limited suit oxygen, and run a colony through a resource simulation. Six resources are linked: electricity, oxygen, water, food, radiation protection and construction materials. For example, a greenhouse needs power and water, solar panels make less power under dust or on Mars, shielding needs materials, and research and communications need electricity. Random events such as a solar storm, dusty panels, a failed oxygen maker or a communication delay force trade-offs, and the player sees the result in the numbers. After each choice, the "Why did this happen?" panel explains the science. After each mission, a debrief shows What You Learned, What Your Decision Changed, The Real Science and a NASA Reference.

BENEFITS

Children practise systems thinking, planning and problem solving. They learn that no decision in space is free. Progress is saved locally with ranks, XP, achievements, daily challenges and collectible history cards, so it works for classrooms and for home play.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want children to see space exploration as something they can understand and take part in, and to build early interest in STEM careers.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js for real-time 3D, the Web Audio API for a generated music score and sound effects, and the browser's speech synthesis for two guide voices (Nova and Mission Control). All 3D models, terrain and textures are generated by code. We also built a test script that ran thousands of simulated playthroughs to check that every mission can be won. SI tools helped us write code and text (see the SI answer).

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It combines open-world exploration, base-building progression, a real spacewalk and a strategy simulation in one story, with an original visual style and a live-generated soundtrack. Education is built into the gameplay, not placed in text blocks.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: every screen labels content as real science, an archived NASA record, educationally simplified, or simulated, and never presents simulated numbers as live NASA readings. Accessibility: subtitles, volume controls, reduced motion and touch controls. Performance: the game lowers its render resolution automatically on slower laptops. Safety: the content is age appropriate.
